"title": "Three-dimensional topological valley photonics",
"authors": "Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang",
"field_subfield": "Photonics / Topological photonics",
"type_of_paper": "Theoretical and experimental",
"executive_summary": "Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where light confinement along the third dimension is achieved non-topologically (e.g., total internal reflection), leading to out-of-plane losses and planar-only light manipulation. This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework featuring a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems with a single pair of valleys characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, the 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a diamond-like lattice composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by adjusting sphere diameters to open a complete photonic bandgap. They theoretically derive an effective k·p Hamiltonian near each valley and demonstrate selective excitation of valley states using a vectorial chiral source array, verifying the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through outcoupling direction measurements at 13.8 GHz. They also demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, revealing the right-hand-thumb rule. The findings highlight potential applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.",

summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.executive_summary: Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where light confinement along the third dimension is achieved non-topologically (e.g., total internal reflection), leading to out-of-plane losses and planar-only light manipulation. This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework featuring a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems with a single pair of valleys characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, the 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a diamond-like lattice composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by adjusting sphere diameters to open a complete photonic bandgap. They theoretically derive an effective k·p Hamiltonian near each valley and demonstrate selective excitation of valley states using a vectorial chiral source array, verifying the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through outcoupling direction measurements at 13.8 GHz. They also demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, revealing the right-hand-thumb rule. The findings highlight potential applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where light confinement along the third dimension is achieved non-topologically (e.g., total internal reflection), leading to out-of-plane losses and planar-only light manipulation. This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework featuring a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems with a single pair of valleys characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, the 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a diamond-like lattice composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by adjusting sphere diameters to open a complete photonic bandgap. They theoretically derive an effective k·p Hamiltonian near each valley and demonstrate selective excitation of valley states using a vectorial chiral source array, verifying the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through outcoupling direction measurements at 13.8 GHz. They also demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, revealing the right-hand-thumb rule. The findings highlight potential applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.

Research Context
Valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control light flow. 2D valley photonic crystals host a single pair of valleys with scalar Chern numbers. Valley-contrasting physics underlies vortex states and edge states. All prior valley photonics studies were limited to two dimensions. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar light manipulation. Full confinement requires a complete photonic bandgap. The complete photonic bandgap remains a significant challenge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can 3D topological valley photonics be realized with a complete photonic bandgap? Do 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys with vectorial Chern numbers? Can vectorial valley-contrasting physics be verified experimentally? Can canalized chiral valley surface states exist on all sample surfaces? Is the propagation direction governed by the right-hand-thumb rule?

Methodological Details
The study combines theoretical modeling and experimental verification. The 3D photonic crystal has a lattice constant of 20 mm. The lattice vectors are defined as a1, a2, and a3. The crystal is a diamond-like lattice with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter 1.2 mm. The rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. Inversion symmetry is preserved when the sphere diameters are equal. The diameters are set to D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm to break inversion symmetry. Breaking inversion symmetry gaps out the nodal lines to form a complete bandgap. The six valleys are located at Wx±, Wy±, and Wz±. The valleys are grouped pairwise due to time-reversal symmetry. The effective Hamiltonian is derived using the k·p method. The mass term is induced by breaking the inversion symmetry. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources with specific positions. The source phase delays are set to form clockwise or counterclockwise winding. The (001) surface is covered with a metallic plate to satisfy the boundary condition. The boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. The metallic plate features perforations with a hole interval of a/2. The sample supports surface states on (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The propagation directions are locked to each valley.

Procedures And Architectures
The band structure is computed for the 3D photonic crystal. Nodal lines form intersecting nodal chains when inversion symmetry is preserved. The momentum of the six valleys is specified for each valley type. The eigenstates display vortex profiles with opposite chirality. The Berry curvature has a nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. The valley Chern vector is calculated by integrating the Berry curvature. The valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The topological chiral surface states satisfy the boundary condition. The boundary condition operator is defined with a phenomenological angle. The chiral surface state is determined by the VCV with linear dispersion. The surface dispersion is given by the cross product of the wavevector and VCV. The surface states traverse the bandgap with linear dispersion. The surface transmission is measured to verify the surface states. The bulk transmission is substantially lower than the surface transmission. The surface field distribution is mapped and Fourier-transformed. The surface states exhibit canalization behavior along the +y direction. The canalization is due to the flat isofrequency contour. The canalization is confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The source is positioned at the center of the (001) surface. The field distributions are measured on the (001) and (010) surfaces. The surface states pass through the sharp corner with high transmission. The Fourier transform reveals the valley-locking property. The VCV and circulating direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The right-hand-thumb points to the VCV direction. The curling fingers point to the circulating direction. The right-hand-thumb rule applies to all sample surfaces. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian.

Key Results
The 3D photonic crystal exhibits a complete photonic bandgap. The 3D valley system has six valleys grouped into triple pairs. The eigenstates display vortex profiles with opposite chirality. The Berry curvature verifies vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The outcoupling direction is measured at 13.8 GHz. The clockwise phase winding corresponds to −32.9°. The counterclockwise phase winding corresponds to +32.9°. The case without phase winding corresponds to 0°. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The valley Chern vector is calculated by integrating the Berry curvature. The chiral surface state is determined by the VCV with linear dispersion. The surface states traverse the bandgap with linear dispersion. The surface transmission is high within the complete photonic bandgap. The bulk transmission is substantially lower than the surface transmission. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction. The canalization is due to the flat isofrequency contour. The sample supports surface states on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. The surface states form a closed loop without intervalley scattering. The right-hand-thumb rule relates the VCV and circulating direction. The Wx− valley carries a VCV (−1/2, 0, 0). The valley surface states circulate clockwise on the y-z plane. The surface states pass through the sharp corner with high transmission. The valley-locking property is experimentally revealed. The right-hand-thumb rule applies to all sample surfaces.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D framework goes beyond the binary valley degree of freedom. The 3D systems exhibit vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The vectorial nature of the 3D valley states is revealed. The vectorial nature highlights potential applications in 3D waveguiding. The orbital moments control the angular momentum of light. The directional outcoupling serves as a mechanism for narrow-beam antennae. The canalized surface states inspire 3D topological photonic devices. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges. All-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals have complete bandgaps.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is demonstrated at lower frequencies. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies. The canalization has been explored at the topological transition point. The canalization is an intrinsic property of the surface states. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The metallic plate features perforations for inserting the source and probe.

Claims
3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics can be realized. The 3D photonic crystal exhibits a complete photonic bandgap. The 3D valley system has six valleys grouped into triple pairs. The vectorial valley-contrasting physics is verified. The canalized chiral valley surface states are demonstrated. The study is demonstrated at lower frequencies. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical ranges. All-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals have complete bandgaps. The applications include 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging.
The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states are governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction are governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The right-hand-thumb points to the VCV direction. The curling fingers point to the circulating direction. The right-hand-thumb rule applies to all sample surfaces. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The applications include 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the 3D VPC characterized by vectorial Berry curvatures. Figure 2 shows the selective excitation of vectorial valley states. Figure 3 shows the observation of the canalized chiral valley surface states. Figure 4 shows the right-hand-thumb rule relating the robust chiral valley surface states with the VCVs.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of 3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration of canalized chiral valley surface states on all sample surfaces. 3. The future path is the extension of the concept to terahertz and optical ranges.
